data: Second Shuttle; lost 73s after launch on STS-51-L 1986-01-28 with 7 crew

Built from a structural test article (STA-099) converted to flight configuration when Enterprise was deemed too expensive to upgrade. First flight STS-6 (1983-04-04) — the first Shuttle EVA. Flew 10 missions before being lost. STS-51-L (1986-01-28) launched at unprecedented cold (−1 °C), causing the right SRB's O-rings to fail seal; hot gas burned through the strut attaching the SRB to the external tank, the tank ruptured, and the orbiter broke apart at Max-Q (T+73s) at 14 km altitude. The crew compartment fell intact and impacted the Atlantic ~2:45 later; all seven crew (Smith, Scobee, Resnik, McNair, Onizuka, Jarvis, McAuliffe) perished. The Rogers Commission ground the Shuttle for 32 months and rewrote NASA's safety culture — every subsequent program design dates to lessons learned here.
STS-6 (1983-04-04) · first Challenger flight; first Shuttle EVA (Musgrave + Peterson) · deployed TDRS-1
STS-41-B (1984-02-03) · first untethered EVA — McCandless and Stewart on MMU jetpacks
STS-41-G (1984-10-05) · first 7-person crew; first US-female EVA (Sullivan); Sally Ride's 2nd flight
STS-51-L (1986-01-28) · LOST 73 s after launch — right SRB O-ring failure in unprecedented cold (−1°C); all 7 crew (Scobee, Smith, Resnik, Onizuka, McNair, Jarvis, McAuliffe) perished
OV-099 — second operational Shuttle. Lost 73s after launch on STS-51-L (1986-01-28) with all seven crew including teacher Christa McAuliffe

Challenger, OV-099, was the fleet's early workhorse and the site of its first catastrophe. It flew the program's first spacewalk and carried the first American woman, Sally Ride, to orbit. On 28 January 1986, launching in unusually cold weather, a rubber seal in one of its solid boosters — stiffened by the cold, a failure mode engineers had warned of — gave way, and the vehicle broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff. All seven aboard died. The disaster grounded the fleet for nearly three years and exposed a management culture that had flown past a known, flagged risk.

Built from a structural test article (STA-099) converted to flight after Enterprise was deemed too expensive to upgrade. First flew STS-6 (1983-04-04) carrying out the first Shuttle EVA. Flew 10 missions in total: STS-6, STS-7, STS-8, STS-41-B, STS-41-C, STS-41-G, STS-51-B, STS-51-F, STS-61-A, and final flight STS-51-L. On 1986-01-28, STS-51-L launched at unprecedented cold (−1 °C) — the right SRB's O-rings failed to seal, hot gas burned through the strut attaching the SRB to the external tank, and the orbiter broke apart at Max-Q (T+73s) at 14 km altitude. All seven crew perished, including teacher Christa McAuliffe. The Rogers Commission grounded the Shuttle for 32 months and rewrote NASA's safety culture.
OV-103 — third Shuttle. Deployed Hubble (STS-31, 1990); flew both return-to-flight missions. 39 missions — most of any orbiter
OV-104 — fourth Shuttle. Flew final mission STS-135 (2011), final Hubble servicing STS-125 (2009), deployed Galileo + Magellan
OV-102 — the first Shuttle orbiter to fly to space (STS-1, 1981-04-12); lost on re-entry STS-107 2003-02-01
OV-101 — prototype Shuttle. Renamed from Constitution after Star Trek fan campaign. Flew 1977 atmospheric tests; never reached orbit
OV-105 — fifth Shuttle, built from spares to replace Challenger. First Hubble servicing STS-61 (1993); delivered Unity + Canadarm2
